 Plantae contains eukaryotic, multicellular but autotrophic organisms which possess cell wall made up of cellulose.
 Animals contain all the eukaryotic, multicellular, heterotrophic but cell wall lacking organisms.

282648.explanation:
Nutrition in monerans may be Autotrophic (chemosynthetic and photosynthetic) or heterotophic (saprophytic/parasitic).
 Nutrition in protists may be Autotrophic (photosynthetic) or heterotrophic.
 Nutrition in fungi is Heterotrophic (saprophytic/parasitic).
 Nutrition in animals is Heterotrophic (holozoic/parasitic).
 Nutrition in plants is autotrophic (photosynthetic). Plants possess cell wall made up of cellulose.

282649.explanation:
Archaebacteria are special since they live in some of the harshest habitats and a group of archaebacteria that can thrive in marshy(anaerobic) areas is known as methanogens.
 Cyanobacteria have chlorophyll a similar to green plants and they are photosynthetic autotrophs.
 Mycoplasma completely lacks a cell wall.
 Plants have their cell wall made up of cellulose.
 Animals are Heterotrophic (holozoic/saprophytic etc.).

282650.explanation:
Trypanosoma is a flagellated protozoan.
 Slime moulds are saprophytic protists.
 Euglena belongs to Euglinoids in the kingdom Protista.
 Chrysophytes include diatoms and golden algae.
 Gonyaulax is an example of dinoflagellates and causes red tides in the sea.

282651.explanation:
Marine forms of Amoeboid protozoans have silica shells on their surface.
 In slime moulds, spores possess true walls.
 Instead of cell walls, Euglenoids have a protein-rich layer called pellicle which makes their body flexible.
 Chrysophytes include diatoms and golden algae. In diatoms, the cell walls form two thin overlapping shells, which fit together as in a soapbox. The walls are embedded with silica and thus the walls are indestructible. Thus, diatoms have left behind a large amount of cell wall deposits in their habitat; this accumulation over billions of years is referred to as ‘diatomaceous earth’.
 In Dinoflagellates, the cell wall has stiff cellulose plates on the outer surface.

282652.explanation:
Protozoans are believed to be primitive relatives of animals.
 Slime moulds possess spores with true walls that are dispersed by air currents.
 Euglenoids have pigments that are identical to those present in higher plants.
 Chrysophytes include diatoms and golden algae. In diatoms, the cell walls form two thin overlapping shells, which fit together as in a soapbox. The walls are embedded with silica and thus the walls are indestructible. Thus, diatoms have left behind a large amount of cell wall deposits in their habitat; this accumulation over billions of years is referred to as ‘diatomaceous earth’.
 Red dinoflagellates (Example: Gonyaulax) undergo such rapid multiplication that they make the sea appear red (red tides).

282653.explanation:
Puccinia causes rust disease in wheat.
 Dikaryon is a stage of cells found in life cycles of ascomycetes and basidiomycetes.
 Rhizopus causes bread mould.
 Albugo is commonly known as smut fungi.
 Ustilago is a parasitic fungus on mustard.

282654.explanation:
Plants commonly show alteration of generation.
 In Deuteromycetes, only asexual or vegetative mode of reproduction is found that is why they are known as imperfect fungi.
 Basidiomycetes do not reproduce asexually however vegetative reproduction, commonly, occurs by fragmentation.
 Ascomycetes reproduce asexually by conidia formation.
 In Phycomycetes mycelium is aseptate and coenocytic.

282655.explanation:
Plants reproduce by Sexual, Asexual, and Vegetative reproduction.
 In Deuteromycetes sexual reproduction is not known hence they reproduce only by asexual reproduction.
 In Basidiomycetes asexual spores are generally not found.
 Ascomycetes reproduce asexually by conidia formation.
 In Phycomycetes mycelium is aseptate and coenocytic.

282656.explanation:
D.J. Ivanowsky (1892) recognized certain microbes as causal organisms of the mosaic disease of tobacco.
 M.W. Beijerinek (1898) demonstrated that the extract of the infected plants of tobacco could cause infection in healthy plants and called the fluid as Contagium Vivum fluidum (infectious living fluid).
 The name virus that means venom or poisonous fluid was given by Pasteur.
 T.O. Diener discovered a new infectious agent that was smaller than viruses and caused potato spindle tuber disease. It was found to be a free RNA; it lacked the protein coat that is found in viruses, hence the name viroid.
 W.M. Stanley (1935) showed that viruses could be crystallized and crystals consist largely of proteins. They are inert outside their specific host cell.

282657.explanation: Given figure is showing Aspergillus. It belongs to Ascomycetes in kingdom fungi.

282658.explanation: Protista is a group of all unicellular eukaryotic plants and animals. The organisms included in this group are either photoautotrophs, heterotrophs or parasites. Whereas Monera includes prokaryotic like bacteria, unicellular organism. Fungi are eukaryotic but are mostly multicellular (except yeast which is unicellular).

282659.explanation: Halophiles are organisms that live in areas of high concentration of salts. Whereas, heliophytes are the plants that grow best in sunlight and cannot survive in salty conditions. Methanogens are the bacteria that produce methane as a metabolic by products in anaerobic conditions. Thermoacidophiles are archaebacteria striving under strong acidic environments and high temperatures, but cannot tolerate high salt concentrations around them.

282660.explanation: A dikaryon is a stage when a cell contains two nuclei and this condition occurs when the cytoplasm of two haploid cells gets fused but nuclei do not.

282661.explanation: M.W Beijerinek proposed Contagium vivum fluidum means contagious living fluid. This phrase was first used to describe virus, characteristic in escaping from the finest mesh available. D. J Ivanowsky was a Russian Botanist who discovered the filterable nature of viruses and one of the founders of virology. Stanley Miller was a Jewish American chemist who experimented on origin of life. Robert Hooke was the first to study and record cells using his primitive microscope.

282662.explanation: Mycobiont and phycobiont are found in lichens. Lichens are dual organisms which has a permanent symbiotic association of fungus and an alga. The fungal partner is called mycobiont and the algal partner is called phycobiont. Mycorrhiza is association of fungus with roots, but not with an alga, while BGA is blue green alga a member of Monera having a prokaryotic cell.

282663.explanation:
A virus is a nucleoprotein and the genetic material is infectious. Protein forms body coat inside which genetic material is placed.
 While, Viroid was found to be a free RNA; it lacked the protein coat that is found in viruses, hence the name viroid.

282664.explanation: Viruses did not find a place in classification since they are not considered truly ‘living’ if we understand living as those organisms that have a cell structure. The viruses are non-cellular organisms that are characterized by having an inert crystalline structure outside the living cell.

282665.explanation: Phycomycetes are the members of fungi that can thrive well on dead and decaying wood as saprophytes. These prefer to live in moist and damp places and need water for the movement of zoospores and sexual gametes. Few members of phycomycetes are obligate parasites like Phytophthora infestans causing late blight of potato and Peronospora sp. causing downy mildew of grapes.

282690.explanation: Mycoplasma is an organism that completely lacks a cell wall. They are the smallest living cells known and can survive without oxygen. Many mycoplasmas are pathogenic in animals and plants.

282691.explanation: Gram +ve bacteria contain several layers of mucopeptide while gram -ve bacteria contain a single layer of mucopeptide or murein.

282692.explanation: Clostridium botulinum is an anaerobic, rod-shaped spore-forming bacterium that produces a protein with characteristic neurotoxicity. Under certain conditions, these organisms may grow in foods producing toxin(s). Botulism, a severe form of food poisoning results when the toxin-containing foods are ingested.

282693.explanation: Muramic acid is an amino sugar acid. In terms of chemical composition, it is the ether of lactic acid and glucosamine. It occurs naturally as N-acetylmuramic acid in peptidoglycan, whose primary function is a structural component of many typical bacterial cell walls.

282694.explanation: Some phages are able to “mobilize” bacterial genes and carry them from one bacterial cell to another through the process of transduction.

282695.explanation: The bacterial chromosome is one long, single molecule of double-stranded, helical, supercoiled DNA. In most bacteria, the two ends of the double-stranded DNA covalently bond together to form both a physical and genetic circle.

282696.explanation: A chemolithotroph is an organism that is able to use inorganic reduced compounds as a source of energy. They oxidize the inorganic compounds in the presence or absence of oxygen to produce ATP. This mode of metabolism is known as chemolithotrophy.

282697.explanation: Bacterial cell walls are made of peptidoglycan (also called murein), which is made from polysaccharide chains cross-linked by unusual peptides containing D-amino acids.

282698.explanation: Bacterial DNA binding proteins are a family of small, usually basic proteins of about 90 residues that bind DNA and are known as histone-like proteins. Since bacterial binding proteins have a diversity of functions, it has been difficult to develop a common function for all of them. They are commonly referred to as histone-like and have many similar traits with the eukaryotic histone proteins.

282699.explanation: Antony Leeuwenhoek was the first person to see bacteria.

282700.explanation: The plasmid is a small circular, extrachromosomal and self-replicating double-stranded DNA molecule found in bacterial cells. The plasmid is used as a vector in genetic engineering to carry foreign DNA molecules into a host.

282701.explanation: The rabies virus genome is single-stranded, antisense, nonsegmented, RNA of approximately 12 kb.

282702.explanation: The unequivocal proof that DNA is the genetic material came from the experiments of Alfred Hershey and Martha Chase (1952). They worked with viruses that infect bacteria called bacteriophages. The bacteriophage attaches to the bacteria and its genetic material then enters the bacterial cell. The bacterial cell treats the viral genetic material as if it was it's own and subsequently manufactures more virus particles. Hershey and Chase worked to discover whether it was protein or DNA from the viruses that entered the bacteria.

282703.explanation: Enterobacteria phage T2 (Coliphage T2) is a virus that infects and kills E.coli. It is in the genus Tequatrovirus, and the family Myoviridea. Its genome consists of linear double-stranded DNA, with repeats at either end. The phage is covered by a protective protein coat.

282704.explanation: Pasteur was the first to propose that diseases were caused by microscopic organisms. The final proof of germ theory came when Pasteur was able to grow the anthrax bacillus in culture. Although anthrax had been isolated by Robert Koch, opponents believed that the spores he found could have been containments in his culture medium. Pasteur placed a drop of blood from a sheep dying of anthrax into a sterile culture and allowed the bacilli to grow. He repeated this process until none of the original cultures remained in the final dish. The final culture produced anthrax when injected into sheep, showing that the bacillus was responsible for the disease.

282705.explanation: Bacteriophage ΦX174 is a small icosahedral virus that contains a single-stranded, closed circular DNA molecule with 5,386 nucleotide bases.

282706.explanation: E.coli is a bacteria (prokaryotic cell) and hence has a single chromosome because all prokaryotic cells have a single chromosome.

282707.explanation: Viroids are composed solely of a short strand of circular, single-stranded RNA without protein coat.

282708.explanation: Clostridium is a non-symbiotic anaerobic non-photosynthetic nitrogen-fixing bacterium.

282709.explanation: Cyanophages are viruses that infect cyanobacteria. They have linear double-stranded DNA as the genetic material.

282710.explanation: Bacteria are considered as plants because these have a rigid cell wall.

282712.explanation: Nitrogen fixation is a process by which molecular nitrogen in the air is converted into ammonia (NH3) or related nitrogenous compounds in soil. Hence, Bacteria that convert the nitrogen of the air to nitrogenous compounds are called nitrogen-fixing bacteria.

282713.explanation: If a bacterium divides once in half an hour then after every half hour the number of bacteria will be twice. Hence after four hours the number of bacteria will be 256 ( 1 to 2, 2 to 4, 4 to 8, 8 to 16, 16 to 32, 32 to 64, 64 to 128, 128 to 256).

282714.explanation: Although viruses are smallest which cause disease among plants. They are acellular structures and are not considered as true living. Hence we can say that mycoplasma is the smallest living organism that causes disease among plants.

282715.explanation: AIDS is a viral disease that spreads through body fluids. These body fluids can be exchanged between individuals by sexual contact, the needle used to multiple persons, or by the immoral way of life (using utensils and other goods of an infected person).

282716.explanation: Mumps is a viral disease caused by the mumps virus.

282717.explanation: Bacteria are grouped under four categories based on their shape: the spherical Coccus (pl.: cocci), the rod-shaped Bacillus (pl.: bacilli), the comma-shaped Vibrium (pl.: vibrio) and the spiral Spirillum (pl.: spirilla).

282718.explanation:
Structurally, the influenza virus is spherical in shape. It is covered in an envelope made of a lipid bilayer with spikes of glycoproteins called haemagglutinin and neuraminidase. These proteins enable the virus to effectively bind with a host cell.

Inside the envelope is the capsid, which is the protein shell we mentioned earlier. Like a time capsule holding precious keepsakes, the capsid contains the genetic information. In the case of influenza, seven or eight strands of RNA are tightly encapsulated, awaiting the time of release into a host cell. The RNA is bound onto coils of ribonuclear proteins or RNPs.

282719.explanation: Nostoc is the free-living nitrogen-fixing cyanobacteria and increases the nitrogen content of moist soil and water bodies, which can be used in increasing paddy yield.

282720.explanation: Bacillus megaterium is a rod-like, Gram-positive, mainly aerobic spore-forming bacterium found in widely diverse habitats. It is used to cure the bitterness of tea leaves.

282721.explanation: Amphitrichous bacteria have a single flagellum on each of two opposite ends (only one flagellum operates at a time, allowing the bacterium to reverse course rapidly by switching which flagellum is active).

282722.explanation: HIV is a retrovirus, which means it carries single-stranded RNA is its genetic material rather than the double-stranded DNA human cells carry. Retroviruses also have the enzyme reverse transcriptase, which allows it to copy RNA into DNA and use that DNA "copy" to infect humans, or host, cells.

282723.explanation: Three human T-lymphotropic viruses have been isolated and characterized in the past 5 years. The ability to culture target cells with T-cell growth factor and sensitive detection systems for the virally encoded polymerase reverse transcriptase permitted isolation of HTLV-I, which is strongly linked to the cause of adult T-cell leukemia and associated with other lymphoid malignancies in endemic areas. The same techniques, using a permissive human tumor cell line, allowed the isolation and characterization of HTLV-III / lymphadenopathy-associated virus, which is implicated as the primary cause of the acquired immunodeficiency syndrome (AIDS).

282724.explanation: Virus-infected cells secrete proteins called interferons which protect non-infected cells from further viral infection. It is a type of cytokine barrier in our body.

282725.explanation: Once viruses infect a cell they take over the machinery of the host cell to replicate themselves, killing the host. These hosts are specific for each type of virus.

282726.explanation: When a virus infects its host, it takes over the machinery of the host to synthesize its protein and copying genetic material. During this process of a virus can also mutate itself. This shows the living nature of the virus.

282727.explanation: A virus is a nucleoprotein (protein with genetic material) and the genetic material is infectious. Bacterial viruses or bacteriophages (viruses that infect the bacteria) are usually double-stranded DNA viruses.

282728.explanation: A virus is a non-cellular, obligatory parasite (i-e; host-dependent), a self-replicating genetic element consisting of DNA and RNA with no metabolic capability, but capable of transmission from the host cell to host cell via a vector stage called Virion in which the nucleic acid is encapsulated in a protein coat.

282729.explanation: Viruses that infect animals have either single or double-stranded RNA or double-stranded DNA. No virus contains both RNA and DNA.

282730.explanation: Leaf roll of potato is a disease caused by virus.

282731.explanation: Shoot apex has meristematic cells that remain free of viral infection. These meristematic cells can be used as explants in tissue culture to grow virus-free plants.

282732.explanation: Measles, rabies are diseases that are caused by viruses.

282733.explanation: Viruses are obligate parasite. They are host-dependent to complete their life cycle.

282734.explanation: Majority of viruses that infect plants have single-stranded RNA.

282735.explanation: Polio (Poliomyelitis) is an infectious disease caused by the poliovirus.

282736.explanation: Pneumonia is caused by a bacteria named Streptococcus pneumonea. Antibodies are only produced to kill bacterial cells. Measles, mumps, and AIDS are viral diseases and hence no antibody is given during these diseases.

282738.explanation: The symptoms of the disease little leaf of brinjal include shortening of the petioles and production of leaves which are much smaller in size. Petioles are so short that leaves seem to be glued to the stem. They become soft and glabrous and somewhat yellow in colour. Affected plants do not bear any flowers or fruits if the infection is in the early stages of plant growth. However, in cases of late-season infections fruits may remain small, become hard, and unfit for consumption or marketing. The disease is caused by a plant pathogenic mollicute, phytoplasma (earlier known as mycoplasma like an organism or MLO), and is transmitted by the insect vector, Hishimonus phycitis which belongs to the group of leafhoppers.

282739.explanation: DPT is a class of combination vaccines against three infectious diseases in humans: diphtheria, pertussis (whooping cough), and tetanus. The vaccine components include diphtheria and tetanus toxoids and killed whole cells of the bacterium that causes pertussis. The vaccine is also known as "DTP" or "DTwP", where the lower-case "w" indicates whole-cell inactivated pertussis.

282740.explanation: Yersinia pestis (formerly Pasteurella pestis) is a gram-negative, non-motile, rod-shaped coccobacillus bacterium, with no spores. It is a facultative anaerobic organism that can infect humans via the oriental rat flea (Xenopsylla cheopis). It causes the disease plague.

282741.explanation: Mesosomes or chondrioids are folded invaginations in the plasma membrane of bacteria.

282742.explanation: At lower temperature activity of enzymes and chemical reactions are adversely affected. Bacterial attack on food is also due to the activity of certain enzymes and the result of certain chemical reactions. Thus the bacterial attack on food is prevented at low temperature and food can be preserved.

282743.explanation: In 1946, Joshua Lederberg and Edward Tatum astonished the genetics world with their discovery that bacteria could exchange genes through a process now known as conjugation. It's really a form of bacterial sex which, oddly enough, is entirely separate from bacterial reproduction.

282744.explanation: Fermented milk products or fermented dairy products, also known as cultured dairy foods, cultured dairy products, or cultured milk products, are dairy foods that have been fermented with lactic acid bacteria such as Lactobacillus lactococcus.

282745.explanation: Asthma is a common long-term inflammatory disease of the airways of the lungs. It is characterized by variable and recurring symptoms, reversible airflow obstruction, and easily triggered bronchospasms. Asthma is thought to be caused by a combination of genetic and environmental factors. Environmental factors include exposure to air pollution and allergens.

282746.explanation: Tuberculosis (TB) is caused by a type of bacterium called Mycobacterium tuberculosis. It's spread when a person with active TB disease in their lungs coughs or sneezes and someone else inhales the expelled droplets, which contain TB bacteria.

282747.explanation: The cell membrane of Gram - ve and + ve bacteria is made up of proteins and phospholipids. The proteins are randomly distributed in the phospholipid bilayer of the cell membrane.

282748.explanation: Rhizobium is a genus of bacteria associated with the formation of root nodules on plants. These bacteria live in symbiosis with legumes. They take in nitrogen from the atmosphere and pass it on to the plant, allowing it to grow in soil low in nitrogen.

282749.explanation: Nitrogen-fixing bacteria, microorganisms capable of transforming atmospheric nitrogen into fixed nitrogen (inorganic compounds usable by plants). More than 90 percent of all nitrogen fixation is effected by these organisms, which thus play an important role in the nitrogen cycle. Two kinds of nitrogen-fixing bacteria are recognized. The first kind, the free-living (nonsymbiotic) bacteria, includes the cyanobacteria (or blue-green algae) Anabaena and Nostoc and genera such as Azotobacter, Beijerinckia, and Clostridium. The second kind comprises the mutualistic (symbiotic) bacteria; examples include Rhizobium, associated with leguminous plants (e.g., various members of the pea family).

282750.explanation: Yellow fever is an acute viral haemorrhagic disease transmitted by infected mosquitoes. The "yellow" in the name refers to jaundice that affects some patients. Symptoms of yellow fever include fever, headache, jaundice, muscle pain, nausea, vomiting, and fatigue.

282751.explanation: E. coli (Escherichia coli), is a type of bacteria that normally lives in human intestines. It's also found in the gut of some animals. Most types of E. coli are harmless and even help keep your digestive tract healthy.

282752.explanation: Azotobacter and Bacillus polymyxa is non-symbiotic nitrogen fixers. They are free-living in soil and helps in converting atmospheric nitrogen into nitrates (usable form for plants).

282753.explanation: Plague is a disease that affects humans and other mammals. It is caused by the bacterium, Pasteurella pestis. Humans usually get plague after being bitten by a rodent flea that is carrying the plague bacterium or by handling an animal infected with the plague.

282754.explanation: A pilus (Latin for 'hair'; plural: pili) is a hair-like appendage found on the surface of many bacteria and archaea. The terms pilus and fimbria (Latin for 'fringe'; plural: fimbriae) can be used interchangeably, although some researchers reserve the term pilus for the appendage required for bacterial conjugation.

282755.explanation: Citrus canker is a disease affecting Citrus species caused by the bacterium Xanthomonas axonopodis. The infection causes lesions on the leaves, stems, and fruit of citrus trees, including lime, oranges, and grapefruit. While not harmful to humans, canker significantly affects the vitality of citrus trees, causing leaves and fruit to drop prematurely; a fruit infected with canker is safe to eat, but too unsightly to be sold.

282756.explanation: W.M. Stanley (1935) first isolated and showed that viruses could be crystallized and crystals consist largely of proteins. They are inert outside their specific host cell.

282757.explanation: W.M. Stanley (1935) first isolated and showed that viruses could be crystallized and crystals consist largely of proteins. They are inert outside their specific host cell.

282758.explanation: Viruses did not find a place in classification since they are not considered truly ‘living’ if we understand living as those organisms that have a cell structure. The viruses are non-cellular organisms that are characterized by having an inert crystalline structure outside the living cell. Once the virus infects a cell it takes over the machinery of the host cell to replicate themselves, killing the host. This shows that the virus is living but inside the host only.

282759.explanation: Cauliflower mosaic virus (CaMV) is a member of the genus Caulimovirus, one of the six genera in the family Caulimoviridae, which are pararetroviruses that infect plants. Pararetroviruses replicate through reverse transcription just like retroviruses, but the viral particles contain ds DNA instead of RNA.

282760.explanation: HIV enters into helper T-lymphocytes (TH), replicates, and produce progeny viruses. The progeny viruses released in the blood attack other helper T-lymphocytes. This is repeated leading to a progressive decrease in the number of helper T-lymphocytes in the body of the infected person. During this period, the person suffers from bouts of fever, diarrhea, and weight loss. Due to a decrease in the number of helper T lymphocytes, the person starts suffering from infections that could have been otherwise overcome such as those due to bacteria especially Mycobacterium, viruses, fungi, and even parasites like Toxoplasma. The patient becomes so immuno-deficient that he/she is unable to protect himself/herself against these infections.

282761.explanation: Phytophthora infestans is an oomycete or water mold, a microorganism that causes the serious potato and tomato disease known as late blight or potato blight.

282763.explanation: Different types of yeasts are used for wine production but Saccharomyces cerevisiae is most common. It can tolerate the toxicity of high concentration of alcohol and sulphur dioxide. Other yeasts are efficient up to a certain concentration (about 15%) of alcohol.

282764.explanation: Heterothallic species have sexes that reside in different individuals. The term is applied particularly to distinguish heterothallic fungi, which require two compatible partners to produce sexual spores, from homothallic ones, which are capable of sexual reproduction from a single organism. Heterothallism was first discovered in the basal lineage zygomycetes, in Phycomyces blakesleeanus, named after Albert Blakeslee, the American discoverer of fungal heterothallism.

282765.explanation: Puccinia is a genus of fungi. All species in this genus are obligate plant pathogens and are known as rusts. The genus contains about 4000 species. Puccinia graminis causes black rust disease in certain cereal crops.

282767.explanation:
Early blight of potato is caused by fungus Alternaria solani.
 Late blight of potato is caused by the funguslike oomycete pathogen Phytophthora infestans.
 Smut of wheat is a seed-borne disease that is caused by the fungus Ustilago tritici.
 Stem rust of wheat caused by fungus Puccinia graminis.

282768.explanation: Citric acid is the most important organic acid produced in tonnage and is extensively used in the food and pharmaceutical industries. It is produced mainly by submerged fermentation using Aspergillus niger from different sources of carbohydrates, such as molasses and starch-based media.

282769.explanation:
Ringworm is a fungal infection of the skin. “Ringworm” is a misnomer, since a fungus, not a worm, causes the infection. The lesion caused by this infection resembles a worm in the shape of a ring hence the name.
 Three different types of fungi can cause ringworm: Trichophyton, Microsporum, and Epidermophyton.

282770.explanation:
Bordeaux mixture is a fungicide for vines, fruit trees, and other plants, composed of equal quantities of copper sulphate and calcium oxide in water.
 DDT(Dichlorodiphenyltrichloroethane) and BHC (Benzene hexachloride) are insecticides, while 2,4-dichlorophenoxyacetic acid is a herbicide.

282771.explanation: The red rust of tea caused by Cephaleuros parasiticus is the algal disease of tea.

282772.explanation: Wheat smut is a seed-borne disease and is caused by Ustilago nuda tritici. This fungus causing loose smut survives as dormant mycelia within the embryo of an infected wheat seed. When the seed germinates, the fungus becomes active again. The fungus develops within the growing point and moves into the developing grain tissue as the wheat plants grow.

282773.explanation: Red rot is the most common disease of sugarcane, caused by the fungus Colletotrichum falcatum.

282774.explanation: Investigations have shown that yeasts require one or more members of the vitamin B complex in order to grow well in chemically defined media. It appears, however, that riboflavin (vitamin B2) is not needed as a constituent of the culture media supporting yeast growth. Since riboflavin is known to play an important role as a respiratory enzyme generally throughout the plant and animal kingdoms, it seems probable that yeasts are able to synthesize this vitamin in amounts sufficient at least for their own requirements. In a preliminary survey of the production of vitamin B2 by some 200 kinds of yeasts, one species has been found to produce extraordinary amounts of riboflavin in synthetic culture media.

282775.explanation: Saccharomycetes (yeast) belongs to the kingdom of Fungi and the division Ascomycota (ascomycetes).

282776.explanation: Cleistothecium is a closed spore-bearing structure in some ascomycetous fungi from which the asci and spores are released only by decay or disintegration. Penicillium (ascomycetous fungi) are of major importance in the natural environment as well as food and drug production.

282777.explanation: Heterothallic species have sexes that reside in different individuals. Rhizopus species grow as filamentous, branching hyphae that generally lack cross-walls (i.e., they are coenocytic). They reproduce by forming asexual and sexual spores. In sexual reproduction, a dark zygospore is produced at the point where two compatible mycelia fuse. Thus we can say that rhizopus is a heterothallic fungus.

282778.explanation: Most of the fungi are saprophytic and store their food matter as glycogen. Glycogen serves as an energy reservoir, being broken down into glucose when needed.

282779.explanation: Genera Plantarum was written by Bentham and Hooker. In this book, a taxonomic system for seed plants was given by Bentham and Hooker.

282780.explanation: Herbert Copeland proposed the four-kingdom classification in the year 1956. The four kingdoms are Monera, Protista, Plantae and animalia. The kingdom monera is comprised of the unicellular organisms. The protists, plants and animals are the eukaryotic organisms.

282781.explanation: The classification in which whole living organisms of the earth are classified as plants or animals is known as the "Two Kingdom classification" system. In this system first form organisms, which have some animal-like and some plant-like characters, do not get a clear position. For example Euglena. According to two kingdom classification, euglena is mobile like animals but autotrophic like plants.

282782.explanation: Cyanobacteria are oxygenic photosynthetic bacteria. They harvest the sun's energy, absorb carbon dioxide, and emit oxygen. Like plants and algae, cyanobacteria contain chlorophyll and convert carbon dioxide to sugar through carbon fixation. Unlike eukaryotic plants and algae, cyanobacteria are prokaryotic organisms. They lack a membrane-bound nucleus, chloroplasts and other organelles found in plants and algae. Instead, cyanobacteria have a double outer cell membrane and folded inner thylakoid membranes that are used in photosynthesis.

282783.explanation: Trichodesmium erythraeum is a species of cyanobacteria that are unique in being visible to the naked eye. This species is also known as "sea sawdust". It is a red coloured blue-green alga which is responsible for the red colour of the Red Sea.

282784.explanation: Some bacteria form mycelia like a mass of filaments and are known as mycelial bacteria. Actinomycetes are Gram-positive mycelial bacteria, known to produce a wide variety of industrially and medically relevant compounds (antibiotics, chemotherapeutics, fungicides, herbicides, and immunosuppressants).

282785.explanation: During rainy seasons, the ground becomes slippery due to the dense growth of cyanobacteria (Blue-green algae). Cyanobacteria are bacteria that obtain energy through photosynthesis. Cyanobacteria synthesize a gelatinous mass around themselves, enclosing multiple filaments. This causes the surface area on which they thrive to be slippery.

282786.explanation: Above mentioned groups of bacteria belong to archaebacteria. The cell wall of archaea is composed of S-layers and lacks peptidoglycan molecules with the exception of methanobacteria who have pseudo peptidoglycan in their cell wall.

282787.explanation: Since there is no synapsis to diploidy in Blue-green algae, there is no meiosis either. So there is no sexual reproduction of any kind is found in archaebacteria.

282788.explanation: Cyanobacteria is an autotrophic bacteria and hence lacks a nucleus and all membrane-bound organelles. Cyanobacteria carry out photosynthesis within the infoldings of the plasma membrane which are known as thylakoid.

282789.explanation: Rickettsia is a genus of non-motile, Gram-negative, non-spore forming, highly pleomorphic bacteria that may occur in the forms of cocci, bacilli, or threads. The term "rickettsia" has nothing to do with rickets which is a deficiency disease resulting from lack of vitamin D the bacterial genus Rickettsia was named after Howard Taylor Ricketts in honour of his pioneering work on tick-borne spotted fever.

282790.explanation: Bacillariophyceae (diatoms) Class of unicellular algae, usually occurring singly, but maybe colonial or filamentous. Diatomite is a friable light-colored sedimentary rock that is mainly composed of the siliceous skeletal remains of diatoms. It is a very porous rock with fine particle size and low specific gravity.

282791.explanation: Nostoc is a genus of cyanobacteria found in various environments that forms colonies composed of filaments of moniliform cells in a gelatinous sheath.

282792.explanation: Dinoflagellates are called fire algae because some forms of these protists are bioluminescent, meaning that they are living organisms that produce and emit light. They have pigment luciferin, which is acted upon by the enzyme luciferase causing the production of light without any heat.

282793.explanation: Diatoms are used for the construction of soundproof rooms because their cell wall is made up of silica and silica is good to reduce noise.

282813.explanation: Potato wart is a serious disease, caused by a soil-borne fungus, Synchytrium endobioticum. It is an obligate parasite, which does not produce mycelium but an abundance of dissemination sporangia which is responsible for tumor formation on underground potato organs.

282814.explanation: Neurospora is a genus of Ascomycete fungi. Neurospora is also known as the “Drosophila of the plant kingdom” as it is used as a Model Organism for studies in genetic analysis. Neurospora is actively used in genetic studies and molecular research around the World. Since it is used extensively in genetic studies just like Drosophila melanogaster.

282815.explanation: Cochliobolus miyabeanus (formerly known as Helminthosporium oryzae) is a fungus that causes brown spot disease in rice. This disease was the causal agent of the Bengal famine of 1943. It was considered for use by the USA as a biological weapon against Japan during World War II.

282816.explanation: Puccinia is a genus of fungi. All species in this genus are obligate plant pathogens and are known as rusts. The life cycle of Puccinia (also called the "rust cycle") was discovered by Prof. K.C. Mehta.

282817.explanation: Ergot, a fungal disease of cereal grasses caused by species of the ascomycete fungus Claviceps. The disease decreases the production of viable grains by infected plants and can contaminate harvests.

282818.explanation: A clamp connection is a hook-like structure formed by growing hyphal cells of certain fungi. It is created to ensure each cell, or segment of hypha separated by septa (cross-walls), receives a set of differing nuclei, which are obtained through the mating of hyphae of differing sexual types. Clamp connections are structures unique to the phylum Basidiomycota. Many fungi from this phylum produce spores in basidiocarps (fruiting bodies, or mushrooms), above ground. Though clamp connections are exclusive to this phylum, not all species of Basidiomycota possess these structures.

282819.explanation: The Potato spindle tuber viroid (PSTV) was the first viroid to be identified. PSTV is a small, single-stranded circular RNA molecule.

282820.explanation: Scrapie is a fatal, degenerative disease affecting the nervous systems of sheep and goats. It is one of several transmissible spongiform encephalopathies( a group of progressive, invariably fatal, conditions that are associated with prions and affect the brain (encephalopathies) and nervous system of many animals), and as such it is thought to be caused by a prion. Scrapie has been known since 1732 and does not appear to be transmissible to humans.

282821.explanation:
The cryptogram of the virus is the descriptive code summarising the main properties of a virus. The viruses have been named by a system of nomenclature as designated by the International Committee of Virus Nomenclature. It consists of two parts. The first part is the common name of the virus and the second part consists of coded information of it.

Cryptogram of TMV: R/1: 2/5: E/E: S/X.

282822.explanation: Red rot disease is caused by the fungus Glomerella tucumanensis.

282823.explanation: Transduction is the process by which foreign DNA is introduced into a cell by a virus or viral vector. When the DNA is transferred from one bacterium to another with the help of a virus or viral vector-like bacteriophage it is known as bacterial transduction.

282824.explanation: After infection, viral RNA is reversely transcribed to complementary DNA with the help of RNA dependent DNA polymerase enzyme. At this stage, we can see the viral DNA during the life cycle of retroviruses.

282825.explanation: The disease is caused by a plant pathogenic mollicute, Phytoplasma (earlier known as mycoplasma like an organism or MLO), and is transmitted by the insect vector, Hishimonus phycitis which belongs to the group of leafhoppers.

282827.explanation: Methanogens are microorganisms that produce methane as a metabolic byproduct in hypoxic conditions. They are prokaryotic and belong to the domain of archaea. Methanogens identified in the rumens of cattle and sheep and also present in cattle dung.

282828.explanation: Cyanobacteria are microscopic bacteria found in freshwater lakes, streams, oceans, damp soil, moistened rocks. It consists of two groups of photosynthetic eubacteria: the blue-green bacteria (formerly known as blue-green algae, or Cyanophyta), which comprise the vast majority of members, and the grass-green bacteria, or chloroxybacteria.

282829.explanation: Self-assembly of virus capsids follows two basic patterns: helical symmetry, in which the protein subunits and the nucleic acid are arranged in a helix, and icosahedral symmetry, in which the protein subunits assemble into a symmetric shell that covers the nucleic acid-containing core.

282830.explanation: Chlamydomonas and Chlorella are unicellular algae (eukaryotic organisms). Being unicellular and eukaryotic, they are placed in the kingdom Protista.

282831.explanation: Archaebacteria are special since they live in some of the harshest habitats such as extreme salty areas (halophiles), hot springs (thermoacidophiles), and marshy areas (methanogens). Archaebacteria differ from other bacteria in having a different cell wall structure and this feature is responsible for their survival in extreme conditions. In the subdivision Euryarchaeota, uncultivated organisms in deep-sea marine sediments are responsible for the removal of methane a potent greenhouse gas, via anaerobic oxidation of methane stored in these sediments.

282832.explanation: R.H. Whittaker (1969) proposed a Five Kingdom Classification. The kingdoms defined by him were named Monera, Protista, Fungi, Plantae, and Animalia. The main criteria for classification used by him include cell structure, body organization, mode of nutrition, reproduction, and phylogenetic relationships. The mode of reproduction is excluded from the criteria for classification used by R H Whittaker.

282833.explanation: Hallucinogens are a diverse group of drugs that alter a person's awareness of their surroundings as well as their own thoughts and feelings. All Amanita muscaria varieties, but in particular A. muscaria var. muscaria, are noted for their hallucinogenic properties, with the main psychoactive constituents being the neurotoxins ibotenic acid and muscimol.

282834.explanation: Archaebacteria are special since they live in some of the most harsh habitats such as extreme salty areas (halophiles), hot springs (thermoacidophiles), and marshy areas (methanogens). Archaebacteria differ from other bacteria in having a different cell wall structure and this feature is responsible for their survival in extreme conditions.

282835.explanation: The tobacco mosaic virus has a rod-like appearance. Its capsid is made from 2130 molecules of coat protein and one molecule of genomic single-strand RNA, 6400 bases long. The coat protein self-assembles into the rod-like helical structure around the RNA, which forms a hairpin loop structure.

282836.explanation: In addition to proteins, viruses also contain genetic material, that could be either RNA or DNA. No virus contains both RNA and DNA. A virus is a nucleoprotein and the genetic material is infectious.

282837.explanation:
Alternaria is a fungus that belongs to Deuteromycetes. Commonly known as imperfect fungi because only the asexual or vegetative phases of these fungi are known.
 Mucor belongs to Phycomycetes.
 Agaricus belongs to Basidiomycetes but it is a saprophytic fungus.
 Phytophthora is an oomycete that forms a distinct phylogenetic lineage of fungus-like eukaryotic microorganisms.

282838.explanation:
Anabaena is a genus of filamentous cyanobacteria that exist as plankton. As we know that bacteria are prokaryotic organisms hence Anabaena lacks a nucleus.
 Mucor is a fungus while volvox and vaucheria are algae. These three are eukaryotic organisms hence have a well-defined nucleus.

282839.explanation: Morels and truffles differ widely in their form and behaviour. The morels resemble mushrooms to the extent that they have a cap borne upon a central stem, whilst the truffles form solid, round balls, which grow underground. These are the edible ascomycetes.

282840.explanation: Chrysophytes include diatoms and golden algae (desmids). In diatoms, the cell walls form two thin overlapping shells, which fit together as in a soapbox. The walls are embedded with silica and thus the walls are indestructible.

282841.explanation: Monera includes all prokaryotic organisms(cells). Prokaryotic organisms(cells) lack a nucleus and all membrane-bound organelles.

282842.explanation: The viroids were discovered by T.O.Diener in 1971.

282843.explanation: Mucor is a member of Zygomycetes (the conjugation fungi) in which motile cells e.g., zoospores, planogametes, etc. are absent. Asexual reproduction takes place by the formation of nonmotile mitospores called sporangiospores. Sexual reproduction takes place by the formation of nonmotile zygospores.

282844.explanation: Deuteromycetes are commonly known as imperfect fungi because only the asexual or vegetative phases of these fungi are known. Some members are saprophytes or parasites while a large number of them are decomposers of litter and help in mineral cycling.

282845.explanation: Eubacteria are also called true bacteria. Eu stands for true.

282846.explanation: Methanogens are microorganisms that produce methane as a metabolic byproduct in hypoxic conditions. Biogas is the mixture of gases produced by the breakdown of organic matter in the absence of oxygen (anaerobically), primarily consisting of methane and carbon dioxide. Thus methanogens are the primitive prokaryotes responsible for the production of biogas from the dung of ruminant animals.

282847.explanation: Protista includes all the unicellular eukaryotic organisms. As Chrysophytes, Euglenoides, Dinoflagellates, and Slime moulds are unicellular eukaryotic organisms, they are included in the kingdom Protista.

282848.explanation: Viroids were found to be a free RNA; it lacked the protein coat that is found in viruses, hence the name viroid. The RNA of the viroid was of low molecular weight. VIroids are smaller than viruses and they are infectious in nature.

282849.explanation: The fungal cell wall is a complex and flexible structure composed basically of chitin, α- and β- linked glucans, glycoproteins, and pigments.

282850.explanation: Methanogens are microorganisms(bacteria) that produce methane as a metabolic byproduct in hypoxic conditions. Archaebacteria are special since they live in some of the most harsh habitats (like hypoxic conditions).

282851.explanation: In diatoms, the cell walls form two thin overlapping shells, which fit together as in a soapbox. The walls are embedded with silica and thus the walls are indestructible.

282852.explanation: Cell wall in fungi is composed of chitin, a polysaccharide comprising N-acetyl-D-glucosamine (a derivative of glucose).

282853.explanation: In 1971, T.O. Diener discovered a new infectious agent that was smaller than viruses and caused potato spindle tuber disease. It was found to be a free RNA; it lacked the protein coat that is found in viruses, hence the name viroid. The RNA of the viroid was of low molecular weight.

282854.explanation: Archaebacteria are special since they live in some of the most harsh habitats such as extreme salty areas (halophiles), hot springs (thermoacidophiles), and marshy areas (methanogens).

282855.explanation: The Mycoplasma are organisms that completely lack a cell wall. They are the smallest living cells known and can survive without oxygen. Many mycoplasmas are pathogenic in animals and plants.

282856.explanation: Saccharomyces (yeast) are eukaryotic, single-celled microorganisms classified as members of the fungus kingdom.

282857.explanation: Diatoms are microscopic and float passively in water currents (plankton). Diatoms are the chief ‘producers’ in the oceans.

282858.explanation: Ciliates such as Paramoecium differs from other protozoans in having two types of nuclei i.e., macronucleus and micronucleus.

282859.explanation: Many species of Porphyra, Laminaria, and Sargassum are among the 70 species of marine algae used as food. Chlorella and spirulina a unicellular alga rich in proteins is used as food supplements even by space travelers.

282860.explanation: Algae are chlorophyll-bearing, simple, thalloid(undifferentiated body design), autotrophic, and largely aquatic (both freshwater and marine) organisms. They occur in a variety of other habitats: moist stones, soils, and wood. Some of them also occur in association with fungi (lichen) and animals (e.g., on sloth bear).

282861.explanation: Algae are chlorophyll-bearing, simple, thalloid, autotrophic, and largely aquatic (both freshwater and marine) organisms. They occur in a variety of other habitats: moist stones, soils, and wood. Some of them also occur in association with fungi (lichen) and animals (e.g., on sloth bear).

282862.explanation: The form and size of algae are highly variable, ranging from colonial forms like Volvox and the filamentous forms like Ulothrix and Spirogyra. A few of the marine forms such as kelps, form massive plant bodies. Some algae like Chlamydomonas are unicellular.

282863.explanation: The form and size of algae are highly variable, ranging from colonial forms like Volvox and the filamentous forms like Ulothrix and Spirogyra. A few of the marine forms such as kelps, form massive plant bodies.

282864.explanation: Chlamydomonas is a unicellular green algae.

282865.explanation: The form and size of algae are highly variable, ranging from colonial forms like Volvox and the filamentous forms like Ulothrix and Spirogyra. A few of the marine forms such as kelps, form massive plant bodies.

282866.explanation: The algae reproduce by vegetative, asexual, and sexual methods. Vegetative reproduction is by fragmentation. Asexual reproduction is by the production of different types of spores, the most common being the zoospores. They are flagellated (motile) and germination gives rise to new plants. Sexual reproduction takes place through the fusion of two gametes. These gametes can be flagellated and similar in size (as in Ulothrix) or non-flagellated (non-motile) but similar in size (as in Spirogyra).

282867.explanation: The algae reproduce by vegetative, asexual, and sexual methods. Vegetative reproduction is by fragmentation. Each fragment develops into a thallus.

282868.explanation: Spirogyra is green algae and algae reproduce by vegetative, asexual, and sexual methods. Vegetative reproduction is by fragmentation. Each fragment develops into a thallus.

282869.explanation: Asexual reproduction in algae is by the production of different types of spores, the most common being the zoospores which are flagellated (motile) and on germination gives rise to new plants.

282870.explanation: In algae, sexual reproduction takes place through the fusion of two gametes. Isogamous (fusion of similar gametes) sexual reproduction takes place in Chlamydomonas (flagellated), in Spirogyra (non-flagellated). Anisogamous (fusion of dissimilar gametes) in species of Chlamydomonas and oogamous in Volvox, Fucus.

282871.explanation: During sexual reproduction Ulothrix produces flagellated (motile), morphologically similar gametes and Spirogyra produces non-flagellated(non-motile) but morphologically dissimilar gametes. The fusion of morphologically similar gametes is known as isogamous sexual reproduction.

282872.explanation: Volvox and Fucus produce a large, non-motile female gamete and a small, motile male gamete. The fusion between one large, non-motile (static) female gamete and a smaller, motile male gamete is termed oogamous. Thus they show oogamous type of sexual reproduction.

282873.explanation: The pteridophytes have a life cycle with alternation of generations, in which a dominant sporophyte generation produces spores through meiosis, and a free-living gametophyte generation forms gametes, both egg, and sperm, by mitosis. The gametophyte, prothallus is monoecious i.e., it bears both male (antheridia) and female (archegonia) sex organs. Hence, the gametophytes of pteridophytes are short-lived, free-living and bear sexual organs.

282898.explanation: The animals of phylum Porifera are primitive multicellular animals and have a cellular level of organization. Hence, cell aggregates body planning is found in Porifera.

282899.explanation: In Platyhelminthes, the body cavity is absent and hence are called acoelomates.

282900.explanation: Animals possessing coelom are called coelomates. Annelids, molluscs, arthropods, echinoderms, hemichordates and chordates are true coelomates.

282901.explanation: Coelenterates or Cnidarians exhibit tissue level of organisation and are diploblastic.

282902.explanation: Platyhelminthes are acoelomate animals with organ level of organisation.

282903.explanation: The organ system of level of organisation is found in all the mentioned phylum - Annelids, Arthropods and Molluscs.

282904.explanation: Ctenophores are the organisms with tissue level of organisation.

282905.explanation: The organisation in which each system concerned with a specific physiological function is known as organ system level of organisation. In animals like Annelids, Arthropods, Molluscs, Echinoderms, and Chordates have organ -system level of organisation.

282906.explanation: The digestive system in Platyhelminthes has only a single opening to the outside of the body that serves as both mouth and anus and is hence called incomplete.

282907.explanation: The circulatory system in which the blood is pumped out from the heart and the cells and tissues are directly bathed in it, is called open type circulatory system.

282908.explanation: The circulatory system in which the blood is circulated through a series of vessels of varying diameters (arteries, veins and capillaries) is called closed type circulatory system.

282909.explanation: The animals belonging to Phylum Porifera like sponges are mostly asymmetrical, that is, any plane that passes through the centre does not divide them into equal halves.

282910.explanation: Symmetry in which any plane that passes through the centre of body does not divide them into equal halves is called asymmetry.

282911.explanation: When any plane passing through the central axis of the body divides the organism into two identical halves, it is called radial symmetry. Coelenterates, ctenophores, and echinoderms exhibit radial symmetry.

282912.explanation: Organism in which body can be divided into identical left and right halves in only one plane, exhibit bilateral symmetry. Animals like annelids, arthropods, etc., have bilateral symmetry.

282913.explanation: Coelenterates, ctenophores, and echinoderms have radial symmetry in which any plane passing through the central axis of the body divides the organism into two identical halves.

282914.explanation: Animals like Annelids, Arthropods, larva of Echinoderms, exhibit bilateral symmetry in which the body can be divided into identical left and right halves in only one plane.

282915.explanation: An undifferentiated layer called mesoglea, is present in between the ectoderm and the endoderm in diploblastic animals.

282916.explanation: Those animals in which the developing embryo has a third germinal layer, mesoderm, in between the ectoderm and endoderm, are called triploblastic animals. All animals from phylum Platyhelminthes to Chordates are triploblastic.

282917.explanation: Animals in which the cells are arranged in two embryonic layers, an external ectoderm and an internal endoderm, are called diploblastic animals. Coelenterates are diploblastic animals.

282918.explanation: In some animals, the body cavity is not lined by mesoderm, instead, the mesoderm is present as scattered pouches in between the ectoderm and endoderm. Such a body cavity is called pseudocoelom and the animals possessing them are called pseudocoelomates, for example - Aschelminthes.

282919.explanation: In Aschelminthes, the body cavity is not lined by mesoderm, instead, the mesoderm is present as scattered pouches in between the ectoderm and endoderm. Such a body cavity is called pseudocoelom and the animals possessing them are called pseudocoelomates.

282920.explanation: In Platyhelminthes, the body cavity is absent and hence are called acoelomates.

282921.explanation: Animals possessing coelom are called coelomates. Annelids, Molluscs, Arthropods, Echinoderms, Hemichordates and Chordates are coelomates.

282922.explanation: Spongilla is a fresh water sponge belonging to phylum Porifera.

282923.explanation: The members of phylum Porifera are mostly marine and asymmetrical, that is, any plane that passes through the centre does not divide them into equal halves.

282924.explanation: The animals of phylum Porifera have a water transport or canal system in which water enters through minute pores (ostia) in the body wall into a central cavity, spongocoel, from where it goes out through the osculum. Hence, these animals have only the canal system.

282925.explanation: Choanocytes or collar cells are the cells that line the spongocoel and the canals of water transport or canal system in Porifera.

282926.explanation: Leucosolenia is a genus of sponges which have osculum for exit of water in canal system.

282927.explanation: Digestion in Sycon and other sponges is intracellular.

282928.explanation: The members of Porifera are primitive, multicellular animals having cellular level of organisation.

282929.explanation: In Porifera, water enters through minute pores called ostia in the body wall into a central cavity, spongocoel, from where it goes out through the osculum.

282930.explanation: In the water transport system of Porifera, water enters through minute pores (ostia) in the body wall into a central cavity, spongocoel, from where it goes out through the osculum.

282931.explanation: In Porifera, sexes are not separate, that is, they are hermaphrodite. They reproduce asexually by fragmentation and sexually by the formation of gametes. Fertilization is internal and development is indirect having a larval stage which is morphologically distinct from the adult.

282932.explanation: Euspongia is a bath sponge belonging to phylum Porifera.

282933.explanation: Scypha or Sycon is a member of phylum Porifera.

282934.explanation: The cnidoblasts or cnidocytes in Coelenterata contains the stinging capsules or nematocytes on the tentacles and the body. Choanocytes or collar cells line the spongocoel and the canals in Porifera. Hence, options i. and iii. are correct.

282935.explanation: Metagenesis occurs in Obelia which is a cnidarian and exists in both polyp and medusa forms and hence exhibits alternation of generation or metagenesis. The polyps produce medusae asexually and medusae from the polyps sexually.

282936.explanation: Adamsia is correctly matched with its common name sea anemone, belonging to phylum Coelenterata.

282937.explanation: Sea anemone is a diploblastic, acoelomate cnidarian.

282938.explanation: Jellyfish belonging to phylum Coelenterata and starfish belonging to phylum Echinodermata have radial symmetry.

282939.explanation: Hydra, Leech and Tapeworms are hermaphrodite, with each individual having both male and female reproductive organs.

282940.explanation: Hydra is fresh water organism of phylum Coelenterata. It is radially symmetrical and diploblastic animal.

282941.explanation: Hydra exists in both Polyp and Medusa forms which depend upon the nutritional content of the living environment. Medusa is the adult and sexual form whereas Polyp is juvenile and asexual form. Under harsh living conditions and starvation, hydra reproduces sexually.

282942.explanation: The animals of Coelenterata are aquatic, mostly marine, sessile or free-swimming and radially symmetrical.

282943.explanation: The cnidoblasts or cnidocytes contain the stinging capsules or nematocytes in Coelenterata.

282944.explanation: Cnidoblasts in Cnidarians are used for anchorage, defense and for the capture of prey.

282945.explanation: The animals of Colenterata or Cnidarians have a central gastro-vascular cavity with a single opening called hypostome.

282946.explanation: Physalia (Portuguese man-of-war), Adamsia (Sea anemone), Pennatula (Sea-pen) are examples of phylum Coelenterata. They have a central gastro-vascular cavity with a single opening called hypostome.

282947.explanation: In Coelenterates, digestion is both extracellular and intracellular.

282948.explanation: Some of the cnidarians like corals have a skeleton composed of calcium carbonate.

282949.explanation: Polyp is a sessile and cylindrical form found in Corals, Hydra, and Adamsia.

282950.explanation: Aurelia or jelly fish is a medusa form which is umbrella-shaped and free-swimming animal.

282951.explanation: Sessile and cylindrical body form in Cnidarians is known as polyp.

282952.explanation: Umbrella-shaped and free-swimming form in Cnidarians is known as medusa. Example - jelly fish.

282953.explanation: Alternation of generation in which both polyp and medusa stage is present is called as metagenesis.

282954.explanation: In Obelia, both polyp and medusa forms exhibit alternation of generation or metagenesis.

282955.explanation: In metagenesis, polyps produce medusae asexually and medusae form the polyps sexually. Example-Obelia.

282956.explanation: Obelia, Aurelia, and Hydra are aquatic, sessile, or free-swimming, radially symmetrical animals belonging to phylum Cnidaria, and hence all are cnidarians.

282957.explanation: Physalia (Portuguese man-of-war) belongs to phylum Cnidaria.

282958.explanation: Physalia (Portuguese man-of-war), Adamsia (Sea anemone), Pennatula (Sea-pen), Gorgonia (Sea-fan) and Meandrina (Brain coral) are the examples of phylum Coelenterata.

282959.explanation: Pennatula (Sea-pen), Gorgonia (Sea-fan) and Meandrina (Brain coral) are included in Coelenterates.

282960.explanation: In cnidarians, the gastrovascular cavity is also known as the coelenteron or 'blind gut', through which the food enters and waste is excreted out. Adamsia is a Cnidarian hence it has coelenteron.

282961.explanation: The members of Ctenophora are exclusively marine, radially symmetrical, diploblastic organisms with tissue level of organisation.

282963.explanation: Ctenophores are commonly known as sea walnuts or comb jellies which are exclusively marine, radially symmetrical, diploblastic organisms with tissue level of organisation.

282964.explanation: In Ctenophores, the body bears eight external rows of ciliated comb plates, which help in locomotion.

282965.explanation: Eight external rows of ciliated comb plates are found in Ctenophores which help in locomotion of animals.

282966.explanation: Pleurobrachia is a Ctenophore in which digestion is both extracellular and intracellular.

282967.explanation:
Ctenoplana is a Ctenophore in which digestion is both extracellular and intracellular.

Meandrina belongs to phylum Coelenterata where digestion is both extracellular and intracellular. However, the digestive system in snail is intracellular.

282968.explanation: The property of a living organism to emit light is known as bioluminescence. Bioluminescence is well-marked in ctenophores.

282969.explanation: In Ctenophores, reproduction takes place only by sexual means.

282970.explanation: Fasciola belongs to phylum Platyhelminthes. They do not have anus as the alimentary canal consists of a single opening called mouth and therefore, the gut is also called blind gut.

282971.explanation: Platyhelminthes are bilaterally symmetrical, triploblastic and acoelomate animals with organ level of organisation. Example - Flatworms.

282972.explanation: Platyhelminthes are mostly endoparasites having hooks and suckers in the parasitic forms. Some of them absorb nutrients from the host directly through their body surface.

282973.explanation: In Platyhelminthes specialised cells called flame cells help in osmoregulation and excretion. Sexes are not separate. Fertilisation is internal and development is through many larval stages. Some members like Planaria possess high regeneration capacity.

282974.explanation: Taenia (Tapeworm) and Fasciola (Liver fluke) have dorso-ventrally flattened body and hence are included in phylum Platyhelminthes.

282975.explanation: Aschelminthes are bilaterally symmetrical, triploblastic and pseudocoelomate animals. Sexes are separate hence they are dioecious, that is, males and females are distinct.

282976.explanation: The adult worms, Wuchereria bancrofti lives in the lymph nodes and blocks the flow of lymph fluid that leads to the swelling of the limbs. This causes lymphatic filariasis or elephantiasis.

282977.explanation: Aschelminthes is a super-phylum consisting of pseudo-coelomates, They are mostly aquatic, free living or parasitic. Their body is slender, bilaterally symmetrical, and triploblastic.

282978.explanation: Ascaris (Round Worm), Wuchereria (Filaria worm), Ancylostoma (Hookworm) are aschelminthes in which the alimentary canal is complete with a well developed muscular pharynx.

282979.explanation: Round worms may be free living, aquatic and terrestrial or parasitic in plants and animals.

282980.explanation: Fertilisation is internal in round worms and development may be direct in which the young ones resemble the adult or indirect.

282981.explanation: Nereis belongs to phylum Annelida which is an aquatic animal. It is dioecious in which males and females are distinct.

282982.explanation: Nephridia helps in osmoregulation and excretion in phylum Annelida.

282983.explanation: The animals of phylum Annelida exhibit organ-system level of body organisation and bilateral symmetry. They are triploblastic, metamerically segmented and coelomate animals.

282984.explanation: Nereis is an Annelida in which the body surface is marked out into segments or metameres and hence has the metamerically segmented body.

282985.explanation: Annelids may be aquatic (marine and freshwater) or terrestrial; free-living, and sometimes parasitic.

282986.explanation: Aquatic annelids like Nereis possess lateral appendages called parapodia, which help them in swimming.

282987.explanation: Nereis is an aquatic Annelida which is dioecious, that is, male and female are distinct.

283075.explanation:
The correct option is D None of these

The body of all sponges is perforated by having a large number of apertures through which water enters the body and flows through a system of crisscrossing canals. This collectively forms the canal system which is a characteristic feature of poriferans. The flagella of choanocytes beat to produce a water current, which enters the spongocoel through Ostia. It carries food particles and oxygen and sweeps away the metabolic wastes through osculum. Therefore, the canal system serves the function of food collection, respiration and excretion. Some sponges have oviparous fertilization, where sperm and eggs meet in open water. Archaeocytes (or amoebocytes) are totipotent cells in sponges, which can transform into sclerocytes, spongocytes, or collencytes. They have a role in nutrient transport and sexual reproduction. Hence, the option D is the correct answer.

289444.explanation: Bryophytes are nonvascularized plants that are still dependent on a moist environment for survival. Like all plants, the bryophyte life cycle goes through both haploid (gametophyte) and diploid (sporophyte) stages. The gametophyte comprises the main plant (the green moss or liverwort), while the diploid sporophyte is much smaller and is attached to the gametophyte. The haploid stage, in which a multicellular haploid gametophyte develops from a spore and produces haploid gametes, is the dominant stage in the bryophyte life cycle. The mature gametophyte produces both male and female gametes, which join to form a diploid zygote. The zygote develops into the diploid sporophyte, which extends from the gametophyte and produces haploid spores through meiosis. Once the spores germinate, they produce new gametophyte plants and the cycle continues.

Algae are chlorophyll-bearing, simple, thalloid, autotrophic, and largely aquatic (both freshwater and marine) organisms. They occur in a variety of other habitats: moist stones, soils, and wood. The form and size of algae are highly variable, ranging from colonial forms like Volvox and the filamentous forms like Ulothrix and Spirogyra. A few of the marine forms such as kelps, form massive plant bodies. Asexual reproduction is by the production of different types of spores, the most common being the zoospores. They are flagellated (motile) and germinates to gives rise to new plants.

These gametes can be flagellated and similar in size (as in Ulothrix) or non-flagellated (non-motile) but similar in size (as in Spirogyra). Such reproduction is called isogamous. The fusion between one large, nonmotile (static) female gamete and a smaller, motile male gamete is termed oogamous, e.g., Volvox, Fucus. In Chlamydomonas, both isogamous and anisogamous reproduction occurs.

 Numerical taxonomy gave equal importance to all characters as all characters are assigned with numbers and codes and the data are then processed.
 Cytotaxonomy is based on cytological information like chromosome number, structure, behavior.
 Chemotaxonomy uses the chemical constituents of the plant to resolve the confusion.

 Kelps forms profusely branched massive plant body.

 Volvox forms spherical colonies.
